title: The hardest problem on the hardest test
beats: Putnam context: elite students, median score 1-2; hardest problems often have the most elegant solutions
Promise: the video is about how you'd stumble on the solution, not the solution
States problem: 4 random points on sphere, probability tetrahedron contains center; pause to digest
Drop to 2D: 3 points on a circle; names P1,P2,P3 only now
Fix P1,P2, vary P3: lines through center carve 4 arcs; only the opposite arc works
Probability = arc proportion; sweep examples 90 deg, far apart, close together
Average over P2: angles uniform 0-180, proportions uniform 0-0.5, mean 1/4
Same approach in 3D: lines, planes, 8 spherical triangles, opposite one wins
Average size of spherical triangle is hard; surface integral invited but not easy
Back to 2D: why 4? Lesson: reframe the problem around the constructs you added
Re-describe randomness: pick random lines, coin-flip endpoints; same distribution
Pick P3 before coin flips: 4 equal outcomes, exactly one contains center -> 1/4 again
Lift to 3D: 3 lines + P4, 8 coin outcomes, one works -> 1/8
Argument rests on visual intuition; formal linear algebra write-up linked; insight vs formal articulation are separate muscles
Takeaway: ask simpler versions until foothold; reframe around useful added constructs
Sponsor puzzle (cheating students in a circle) and Brilliant pitch

theory: The video teaches by deliberately hitting a wall: the 2D method works, then visibly fails in 3D, which motivates going back and solving the easy case a second, stranger way that scales. The known 2D answer acts as a checksum for the new framing, so the learner trusts the reframe before it is used where it matters.
velocity: Orchestrator: when a method won't generalize, return to the solved small case and re-solve it with a scalable method, verifying against the known answer before lifting
Scene builder: support 'fix some points, drag one' interactions and a dimension toggle (circle<->sphere) with identical construction
Voice: name the meta-heuristic at the pivot moment, not only at the end
Evals: check that a playbook shows the failing natural route before the elegant one
Learner model: flag 'suspiciously clean answer' as a prompt for learners to ask what the number counts
quote: That answer, one-fourth, looks suspiciously clean
